source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2005) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (chapter, ACT-R 5.0)
finding: Core rule of production selection: each production has a utility U = P*G - C. P is the learned chance the goal is reached if it fires, G is the goal value, C is the learned cost (usually time). The highest noisy utility fires.
numbers: Formula U_i = P_i G - C_i. Default goal value G = 20 s in the reference code (see a06).
quote: The highest-valued production is always selected but on some trials one might randomly be more highly valued than another.
limits: Textbook-level statement of the 1998 theory; P and C were later replaced by a reward-difference rule in ACT-R 6 (see a06).
agent_relevance: Operator choice by success rate is exactly this: each operator carries a success estimate and a cost, and the score is value x success minus cost.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2005) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (chapter, ACT-R 5.0)
finding: Choice among matching rules is a softmax over utilities, so worse rules still get sampled sometimes. This keeps the system sensitive to change.
numbers: P(i) = exp(U_i/t) / sum_j exp(U_j/t). Noise parameter t is about 0.5 'in our simulations'; authors call it an emerging reasonable setting.
limits: Value 0.5 is a modelling convention, not a fitted constant across tasks. Fitted values differ (see a13).
agent_relevance: Gives a principled way to keep some exploration of low-scoring operators; the temperature is a knob we must set and test.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2005) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (chapter, ACT-R 5.0)
finding: Success probability is learned as a ratio with a prior. Cost is mean effort per experience. The prior stops the first experience from pushing P to 0 or 1.
numbers: Successes start at prior*V + m, failures at (1-prior)*V + n, where V is prior strength, m and n are observed successes and failures. C = sum of efforts / (successes + failures).
limits: Counts are for goal-level success; credit for multi-step sequences is handled only heuristically (see a09).
agent_relevance: Operator success tracking should start from a prior with a set strength, not from raw 0/0 counts.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2005) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (chapter, ACT-R 5.0)
finding: Building Sticks Task (Lovett): subjects build a target length by adding or subtracting three sticks. Two strategies, overshoot and undershoot, compete. Only one of the two reaches the goal on most problems.
numbers: 15 problems. Both work on problems 1 and 15; only overshoot on 2-8 and 12-14; only undershoot on 9-11. Example: goal 101 with sticks 10, 155, 22 is solved by 155-22-22-10, not by undershoot. Over 80% chose overshoot first on problem 5, where hill-climbing also favored overshoot.
limits: Chapter gives a figure and prose, no raw table; participant N not given in the chapter. One experiment of Lovett's.
agent_relevance: Direct human evidence that strategy choice follows recent success history but is also biased by current-state cues. Both signals should enter operator choice.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2005) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (chapter, ACT-R 5.0)
finding: Lovett's ACT-R model uses four competing rules: always overshoot, always undershoot, choose overshoot if the large stick is closer, choose undershoot if the middle stick is closer. The context rules start slightly higher in utility. Experience then moves utilities.
numbers: By problem 7 the 'decide undershoot' rule has dropped enough that 'always overshoot' wins even where undershoot looks closer. The model also switched quickly at problem 9 and again at 12-14, as people did.
limits: Fit shown graphically; no goodness-of-fit numbers in the chapter.
agent_relevance: Template for operator choice: a few context-triggered operators and a few blind defaults, all scored by one learned utility. The blind default wins once the context cue keeps failing.

source: Gall & Fruehwirth (2014) Exchanging conflict resolution in an adaptable implementation of ACT-R
finding: ACT-R 6 utility learning is a Rescorla-Wagner style difference rule: U(n) = U(n-1) + alpha (R(n) - U(n-1)). Reward R is the external reward minus the time since the rule fired. The older version computed U = P*G - C from success and failure counts.
numbers: Older version: counts start at successes = 1, failures = 0, effort = 0.05 s (one firing). G usually 20 s. Reward is shared by all rules fired since the last reward.
quote: Utility adapts gradually to the average reward a rule receives.
limits: Implementation study in CHR (Prolog), not a behavioral test. Tie-breaking between equal utilities is undocumented and differed between ACT-R 5 and 6.
agent_relevance: Tells us which update rule to copy. The reward-difference rule is recency-weighted; the count rule is stationary. Choose by whether operator success drifts.

source: Gall & Fruehwirth (2014) Exchanging conflict resolution in an adaptable implementation of ACT-R (rock-paper-scissors test)
finding: A rock-paper-scissors test shows the two update rules behave differently. With reward 2 for a win and 0 for a defeat, the reward rule learns to beat a fixed opponent. The success/cost rule with noise off can get stuck.
numbers: Reward rule vs always-rock opponent: final utilities (rock, paper, scissors) = (0, 1.87, -0.02). Vs rock/paper opponent: (0, 0.81, 0.49). Averages over 20 rounds: 10.4 wins, 3.9 draws, 5.7 defeats (opponents 1 and 2). Vs uniform random opponent: 6.6 wins, 6.7 draws, 6.7 defeats. Success/cost rule vs opponent 2: 8.9 wins, 9.1 draws; vs opponent 1 it kept playing rock because a draw gave no update.
limits: 20 samples of 20 moves per opponent (1 sample for opponent 1); noise disabled; not human data.
agent_relevance: A rule whose outcome is neutral never updates, so a bad default can persist. Count 'no progress' as a cost event in our logs.

source: Whitehill (2013) Understanding ACT-R - an outsider's perspective
finding: Critical reading of the 1998 conflict-resolution theory. A matched production fires only if the expected gain from waiting for a better rule does not exceed a waiting cost. Whitehill says the exact process is hard to infer from the book.
numbers: Rule: fire if the integral from V_i to G of (x - V_i) Z_t(x; V_i) dx is at most the waiting cost. V = pG - C; p = q * r, with q learned by a Beta update and r set by heuristics.
quote: the proposed methods of estimating p and C are not optimal, but rather only plausible
limits: Outsider review; points out unclear definitions (density integrates to 1 only if values are bounded above by G; r has two heuristics, cost-so-far or similarity to goal). About the pre-ACT-R-6 theory.
agent_relevance: Do not claim our operator score is 'optimal'; claim it is simple bookkeeping.

source: Whitehill (2013) Understanding ACT-R - an outsider's perspective
finding: Success p is split in two parts. q is the chance the rule's own action works. r is the chance the goal is reached if the action works, set by heuristics tied to effort already spent or distance to goal.
numbers: q updated with a Beta distribution on each success or failure. r falls as cost already spent rises ('hopelessness').
limits: Heuristic, as Anderson himself said. Lovett's model sets effort weight v = 2 (see a11).
agent_relevance: Suggests a two-part score for an operator: did it run correctly, and did it move us toward the goal. We can log both.

source: Whitehill (2013) Understanding ACT-R - an outsider's perspective (power law and strength)
finding: The review finds only a weak link between the theory and the power law of learning, and flags that production strength S(t) = ln(sum_k (t - t_k)^(-d)) + B is defined like chunk activation, with unclear relation to it.
numbers: Same decay form as base-level activation; it is unclear whether B is the same constant.
limits: Critique of the 1998 formulation, not of ACT-R 6/7 code.
agent_relevance: Unused operators lose strength in the theory; dropping stale operators in our scaffold would be a design choice, not an established result.

source: Lovett (1993) Initial ACT-R production system for the Stick Building Task (model source, bst-model.txt)
finding: The original building-sticks model chose, among rule instances, the one with the highest PG-C. P and C came from built-in functions of the rule's history of success (r*) and the instance's distance to the goal.
numbers: File parameters: G = 20; CostScale = 2.5 and EffortScale = 2.5 (half the average path length); distance scale half the goal stick length; v = 2 so effort so far affects r more; parameter learning on, strength learning off.
quote: The model here thus chooses the production instantiation with the highest PG-C.
limits: Written for ACT-R 2.0; the file says the built-in distance function is no longer in the latest ACT-R. Source code, not data.
agent_relevance: The actual recipe: success estimate = rule history combined with a distance-to-goal term. A concrete model of 'history x current context'.

source: Zhu & Simmons (2024) Bootstrapping cognitive agents with a large language model
finding: An LLM writes production rules for an embodied household agent. Choice among matching rules uses ACT-R-style learned utility. A unit reward is given when the agent chooses 'done' and is passed back along the path with a discounted average update, so rules nearer 'done' get higher utility.
numbers: Update: U_after = (N*U_before + gamma^t)/(N+1), gamma = 0.95. Choice: P(rule) proportional to exp(U). No update at all if a subtask ends in 'quit'. Table 1 (text extraction scrambled): find task, action-only LLM 14/15 successes vs rule agent 15/15; slice and clear-countertops 15/15 for both; rule agent used 0 LLM tokens after learning vs tens of thousands for the action-only baseline; paired t-test on steps p = 0.446 (find) and 0.347 (slice).
quote: This utility update process helps reduce the impact of hallucination in LLMs as the knowledge is aggregated.
limits: 15 trials per task; simulated kitchen; per-cell numbers in Table 1 are uncertain. The claim that a good rule always beats a hallucinated one is argued, not tested by an ablation of utility vs random choice.
agent_relevance: Closest LLM paper to our case: success-history utility ranks LLM-written operators. Gives a reward-propagation and discount recipe. No ablation of the utility step is reported.

source: Stocco et al. (2024) Fitting, evaluating, and comparing cognitive architecture models using likelihood
finding: Likelihood fit of ACT-R utility learning to a trial-by-trial two-choice task. A procedural model (two competing rules, utility learned from win $1.0 or loss -$0.5) fit one participant better than a declarative-memory model with the same number of parameters.
numbers: Participant 2, 64 trials, 2 options: chance log-likelihood -44.36; declarative model -35.65 (d = 0.263, s = 0.432); procedural model -30.11 (alpha = 0.759, noise = 0.440). Bayes factor procedural vs declarative = 254.68; declarative vs chance = 6086.09.
limits: One participant shown as a worked example in a primer, not a population test. The fitted alpha 0.759 is far above the 0.2 default.
agent_relevance: Fitted learning rates for people can be large (about 0.76 here). Fit the update rate for operator success on small samples instead of copying 0.2.

source: Stocco et al. (2024) Fitting, evaluating, and comparing cognitive architecture models using likelihood
finding: The primer states the production choice equation as a softmax and the utility update with elapsed time: U_n(p) = U_(n-1)(p) + alpha [R - t - U_(n-1)(p)]. Noise on utility is :EGS; noise on chunk activation is :ANS.
numbers: P(p) = exp(U(p)/s) / sum_i exp(U(i)/s).
limits: Parameter names refer to the ACT-R Lisp implementation.
agent_relevance: Reward is reduced by time spent, so a slow success scores below a fast success. Our budget cost can play the same role.

source: Fan & Lan (2026) From cognitive architectures to language agents: a mechanism-level review
finding: A 2026 review maps ACT-R to language agents. It says learned production utility separates 'can this rule apply' from 'is it worth doing', and that recent LLM-agent work (GraSP, Utility-Guided Agent Orchestration, UALA, KnowNo, Calibrate-Then-Act) rebuilds the idea with calibrated confidence, historical success, gain and cost.
numbers: GraSP calibrates multi-skill routing with historical success and routes low-confidence tasks to ReAct. Utility-Guided Orchestration picks respond, retrieve, tool, verify or stop from gain, cost, uncertainty and redundancy. The review gives evidence grades, no benchmark numbers in the passages I read.
limits: Mapping review with author-run literature screening; no new experiments; I did not open the cited agent papers.
agent_relevance: A list of 2025-26 papers to check for measured results on cost-benefit operator selection. Supports the view that ACT-R utility is a live design idea.

source: Laird (2021) An analysis and comparison of ACT-R and Soar
finding: Compares how the two architectures pick the next action. ACT-R selects one rule by degree of match combined with the rule's utility. Soar proposes and evaluates operators, and an unresolved tie causes an impasse and a substate. Both update utility by temporal-difference learning; in ACT-R all rules fired since the last reward are updated.
numbers: No experimental numbers.
limits: Expert comparison by a Soar author; no new data.
agent_relevance: Soar's impasse is the safety net when scores tie or are missing. Our schema can add an explicit 'tie or no score means gather evidence' step instead of guessing.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) Reinforcement learning for production-based cognitive models (CUNY poster)
finding: Rule ordering in a lexical-decision ACT-R model can be learned by Q-learning instead of hand-coding goal states. Reward +1 at the end, -0.15 for each rule firing.
numbers: Tasks of 1, 2 and 4 stimuli, needing about 12, 18 and 34 steps. 1-stimulus: perfect learning; 2-stimulus: almost perfect; 4-stimulus: learned with some noise.
limits: Poster; no sample statistics; simple lexical decision task, not a human data fit.
agent_relevance: Long chains of operators make credit assignment harder: learning degraded as steps grew from 12 to 34. Keep operator chains short or add intermediate checks.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2020) CUNY poster (open questions)
finding: They name two open questions for production-based models: rule acquisition (production compilation) and rule ordering (utility estimation). They say neither has been applied systematically to complex linguistic models, and that RL and ACT-R have close but largely unexplored connections.
numbers: None.
limits: Position statement in a poster.
agent_relevance: Same split for us: which operators exist vs which operator to pick now.

source: Brasoveanu & Dotlacil (2021) Reinforcement learning for production-based cognitive models (Topics in Cognitive Science)
finding: Seen only as a search snippet: RL agents including deep Q-networks outperformed the standard ACT-R utility learning algorithm on more complex tasks, where ACT-R utility learning was the baseline.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Snippet only; not opened. A lead, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Plain ACT-R utility learning may be too weak for long operator chains.

source: Walsh & Anderson (2011) Learning from delayed feedback: neural responses in temporal credit assignment
finding: Human ERP study of credit assignment over two sequential choices. The feedback-related negativity (a reward-prediction-error signal) followed both final negative feedback and negative intermediate states, so people value intermediate states by expected future reward.
numbers: Temporal-difference models with eligibility traces gave lower BIC than plain actor-critic, Q-learning and SARSA for all but 2 participants; behavior predicted for 13 participants.
limits: Tests generic TD models, not the ACT-R utility equation. Small N (13 modelled).
agent_relevance: Supports crediting earlier operators in a successful chain, with decay, instead of only the last one.

source: Walsh & Anderson (2012) Learning from experience: ERP correlates of reward processing, neural adaptation, and behavioral choice (review)
finding: Review of the feedback-related negativity, read as a reward-prediction-error signal. Four hypotheses tested: it encodes quantitative prediction error; it fires for outcomes and for stimuli that predict outcomes; it and behavior change with experience; it is largest for volitional actions.
numbers: Page text has no mention of ACT-R (count 0), so the link to ACT-R's utility rule is inferred.
limits: Review; neural claim not specific to production rules.
agent_relevance: Weak support for a TD-style update; do not cite as proof of ACT-R's production utility.

source: Taatgen, Lebiere & Anderson (2005) Modeling paradigms in ACT-R (chapter, ACT-R 5.0) (instance learning vs utility)
finding: Utility learning is one of five modeling paradigms. Instance learning (declarative) improves behavior without any evaluation signal; utility learning is needed when there is an evaluation. The sugar-factory model shows what instance learning alone can do.
numbers: Sugar factory (Berry & Broadbent): O(t) = 2W(t) - O(t-1) + random(-1,0,1), goal output 9. People went from 8 to 15 on-target decisions between block 1 and block 2 of 40 trials; the instance model got 9 and 14.
limits: Contrast between the two stores is stated by the authors, not tested in the chapter.
agent_relevance: Keep two stores: a log of cases, and a success rate per operator.

source: Taatgen & Anderson (2002) Why do children learn to say 'broke'? (as described in Taatgen et al. 2005)
finding: Production compilation merges two rules that fire in sequence into one faster rule. The new rule competes by utility with the old ones, so it must earn its place.
numbers: Past-tense example: 'retrieve past tense' plus 'analogy find pattern' compile into 'set answer to word-ed'.
limits: I read only the 2005 chapter's description, not the 2002 paper.
agent_relevance: Operators often used together could be merged into a macro-operator that must beat its parts on success rate.

source: Anderson & Lebiere (1998) The atomic components of thought (book review, Trends in Cognitive Sciences)
finding: Review of the 1998 book: sub-symbolic parameters are updated by experience, so rules and chunks compete by learned value. The reviewer's main worry is lack of parsimony: many mechanisms and many parameters.
numbers: No experimental numbers in the review.
limits: Review of the book, not the book.
agent_relevance: Each added knob (noise, prior strength, goal value) needs its own test; do not import all of them.

source: Gall & Fruehwirth (2014) Exchanging conflict resolution in an adaptable implementation of ACT-R (version differences)
finding: The authors report that the success/cost and reward strategies could not both run in one ACT-R version, and that the tie-break between equal utilities changed between ACT-R 5 and 6.
numbers: Tested on ACT-R 5.0 (success/cost) and ACT-R 6.0 version 1.5-r1451 (reward).
limits: Software compatibility finding.
agent_relevance: Old published model results may not reproduce under newer code. Record parameter set and version when logging operator scores.

source: Lovett & Anderson (1996) History of success and current context in problem solving (Cognitive Psychology 31)
finding: Founding paper for the building-sticks work. Not opened and not found by search; the CV page only confirms the 1994 dissertation title 'History of experience and current context in problem solving'.
numbers: None recorded.
limits: Description of its content rests on a04, a05 and a11 only.
agent_relevance: Primary source to obtain if exact participant counts and effect sizes are needed.

source: Fu & Anderson (2006) From recurrent choice to skill learning: a reinforcement-learning model (J. Exp. Psych: General 135)
finding: Extends ACT-R's utility learning with a temporal-difference rule so credit goes back along a chain of choices. Not opened: the download returned an empty file; the title and aim come from a search snippet.
numbers: None read.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Credit assignment along a chain is the missing piece in the plain utility rule.

source: Stocco et al. (2024) / Zhu & Simmons (2024) compared: where utility is trusted
finding: Across the opened sources the same pattern appears. Human data fits (Stocco) support fast learning and noisy softmax choice; the only LLM-agent use (Zhu & Simmons) adds a discounted, count-averaged update with no noise term beyond exp(U). No source I opened tests utility-based operator choice against random or fixed choice in an LLM agent.
numbers: Gap statement: zero ablations of utility vs random operator choice found among opened LLM papers.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search (budget-limited; APIs were rate-limited).
agent_relevance: Our own test: operator choice by success rate vs fixed order vs random, on the same items.
